question: A real baseband signal has spectral support |f|≤3 kHz. Find its Nyquist rate in samples/s.

steps: The Nyquist rate is twice the upper baseband frequency.
3 kHz is 3000 Hz.
The rate is 2×3000=6000 samples/s; practical ideal-reconstruction sampling is taken strictly above it to avoid endpoint ambiguity.
solution.explanation: The rate is 2×3000=6000 samples/s; practical ideal-reconstruction sampling is taken strictly above it to avoid endpoint ambiguity.
commonMistakes: A Nyquist rate is a boundary; sampling exactly there can lose a component with an unfortunate phase.

hints: Identify the conditions under which nyquist rate applies.
Start from $ f_N=2f_{max} $.

verification.method: Nyquist spectral-replica spacing condition with Hz conversion. Arithmetic checked by executable calculation/property fixtures; same-system solution review only.

question: A 900 Hz cosine is sampled at fs=1000 samples/s. Find its aliased frequency in [0,fs/2], in hertz.

steps: Subtract one sampling frequency: 900−1000=−100 Hz.
For a real cosine, negative and positive frequencies represent the same cosine samples.
The baseband alias is 100 Hz.
commonMistakes: The alias must lie within the first Nyquist interval.

question: Which actions can help avoid irreversible aliasing when sampling an unknown analog baseband input?

options.text: Low-pass filter the analog signal before sampling
Apply a digital low-pass filter only after aliasing has already occurred
Increase the sample rate above twice the passed analog bandwidth
Keep any sample rate and recover lost frequencies by zero padding

steps: Analog low-pass filtering can remove energy that would overlap spectral replicas.
A sufficiently high sampling rate separates those replicas.
Digital filtering or zero padding cannot generally reverse overlap that already merged unknown analog components. Select A and C.
solution.explanation: Digital filtering or zero padding cannot generally reverse overlap that already merged unknown analog components. Select A and C.
commonMistakes: Prevention before sampling is different from smoothing aliased samples later.

hints: Identify the conditions under which analog anti-alias protection applies.

question: A finite observation lasts 0.1 seconds and contains exactly 500 uniformly spaced samples on the half-open interval [0,0.1). Find fs in samples/s.

steps: The half-open interval contains n=0 through N−1 without a duplicate endpoint.
Therefore fs=N/T.
fs=500/0.1=5000 samples/s.
commonMistakes: Including both endpoints would change the sample-count convention.

question: A 300 Hz cosine is sampled initially at 2000 samples/s. Keeping every fourth sample without filtering produces a new sequence. Find its folded baseband frequency in hertz, measured at the new sample rate.

steps: Keeping every fourth sample reduces the sample rate to 2000/4=500 Hz.
The new Nyquist interval ends at 250 Hz, so the original 300 Hz tone folds.
Its baseband alias is |300−500|=200 Hz.
commonMistakes: A signal that was safe at the original rate may alias after decimation.

hints: Identify the conditions under which sample-rate reduction applies.
Start from $ f_{s,new}=f_s/M $.

question: Two real tones at 600 Hz and 1400 Hz are sampled at 2000 Hz. How many distinct nonnegative baseband frequencies do their samples occupy?

steps: The 600 Hz tone already lies below fs/2=1000 Hz.
The 1400 Hz tone folds to |1400−2000|=600 Hz.
Both occupy one frequency location; their phases/amplitudes can combine but cannot make them separately identifiable from sampling alone.

commonMistakes: Two analog tones can collapse to one sampled frequency.

question: An analog signal contains tones only at 1 kHz and 4 kHz. A prefilter passes 1 kHz unchanged and completely rejects 4 kHz, followed by fs=3 ksample/s sampling. What is the highest tone frequency retained in the reconstructed baseband signal, in kHz?

solution.asked: Find the highest retained reconstructed tone.
steps: After the analog filter, only the 1 kHz component remains.
The Nyquist interval extends to 1.5 kHz, so this passed tone does not alias.
Ideal reconstruction retains the 1 kHz tone. The rejected 4 kHz component contributes nothing.
solution.explanation: Ideal reconstruction retains the 1 kHz tone. The rejected 4 kHz component contributes nothing.
commonMistakes: Analyze the analog filter before computing aliases of the remaining spectrum.

hints: Identify the conditions under which prefiltering before sampling applies.
Start from $ f_{pass,max}<f_s/2 $.
